questions.question: What is the defining operational rule of a one-time signature (OTS) keypair?
options: It must sign at most one message securely
It can sign many messages as long as messages are short
It is secure only if the verifier also keeps state
It becomes secure if the hash function output is longer
questions.explanation: OTS schemes are designed to be used once. Reusing the same OTS keypair can leak structure that breaks unforgeability.

questions.question: In a Merkle-tree signature scheme, what does the authentication path provide?
options: Sibling hashes that let you recompute the root from a leaf
A second independent signature for the same message
A way to compress the message before hashing
A shared secret used to randomize the signature
questions.explanation: The authentication path is a Merkle proof: a list of sibling node hashes used to recompute the published root.

questions.question: What is the final validity check performed by LMS verification?
options: The recomputed Merkle root equals the public key root
The signature's randomizer C equals a stored value
The signer index q is less than the message length
The message hash equals the signature bytes
questions.explanation: Verification rebuilds the root from the signed leaf and its authentication path; the signature is valid iff the root matches the public key root.

questions.question: Why is LMS called a stateful signature scheme?
options: The signer must track and never reuse the leaf index q
The verifier must store every signature it has ever seen
The hash function must maintain internal mutable state
The public key changes after every verification
questions.explanation: Each LMS signature consumes a one-time key at index q. If q is reused, security can collapse.

questions.question: Attack scenario: if a buggy signer reuses the same q (same LM-OTS key) to sign two different messages, what is the core security failure?
options: One-time security is violated and attackers may be able to forge additional signatures
The Merkle tree root changes and verification always fails
The scheme becomes deterministic but still unforgeable
Only signature size increases; security is unaffected
questions.explanation: LMS relies on LM-OTS being used once. Reuse can expose enough information for practical forgeries depending on the OTS parameters and attacker capabilities.

questions.question: For LMOTS_SHA256_N32_W8 in this lesson, why is p = 34?
options: 32 coefficients come from Q plus 2 coefficients from the checksum
34 is the Merkle tree height, so it matches the path length
34 is the SHA-256 output size in bytes
34 is chosen to make signatures always a power of two bytes
questions.explanation: With w=8 and n=32, Q contributes 32 bytes (32 coefficients). The checksum contributes 2 more bytes, giving p=34.

questions.question: Which elements are needed to recompute the leaf value during LMS verification?
options: I, q, the message, and the LM-OTS signature
Only the public root and the message hash
Only the authentication path and the public root
Only the LM-OTS public key hash stored in the public key
questions.explanation: The verifier derives an LM-OTS public key candidate from (I, q, message, LM-OTS signature), then hashes it into a leaf and walks up using the path.

questions.question: A signer crashes after emitting a signature but before persisting the incremented q counter. What is the concrete risk after restart?
options: The next signature may reuse the same q and break one-time security
The Merkle tree can no longer be verified by anyone
Old signatures become unverifiable because roots change
Verification becomes slower but security is unchanged
questions.explanation: If the counter update is not atomic, a crash can roll q back and cause leaf reuse, which is a serious security bug for stateful hash-based signatures.
